about: Ext 2 (4U) questions from 2025 trial papers on thsconline, transcribed. Topics: complex numbers, t-formulae, trig sums. 'q' and 'sol' are HTML with KaTeX $...$ delimiters. 'sol' is Claude's worked solution; 'link_q' and 'link_sol' open the original paper page / official solutions in the thsconline viewer. Items have 'base' (5348 = Ext 2 trials, 5338 = Ext 1 trials). 'spage' null means solutions are at the back of that PDF (page unknown). Jamie's school moved t-formulae and product-to-sum into 4U (Ext 2), so those Ext 1 trial questions count as Ext 2 revision.

items.q: Find $\dfrac{-3+i}{1-2i}$, showing all working out.
items.sol:
Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate $1+2i$:
$\dfrac{(-3+i)(1+2i)}{(1-2i)(1+2i)}=\dfrac{-3-6i+i+2i^2}{1+4}=\dfrac{-5-5i}{5}=-1-i$.

items.q: Given that $w=2-i\left(2\sqrt3\right)$ and $\operatorname{Arg}(zw)=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, find the exact value of $\operatorname{Arg}(z)$.
items.sol:
$\operatorname{Arg}(w)=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{-2\sqrt3}{2}\right)=-\frac{\pi}{3}$ (4th quadrant).
$\operatorname{Arg}(z)=\operatorname{Arg}(zw)-\operatorname{Arg}(w)=\frac{\pi}{3}+\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{2\pi}{3}$, which is already in $(-\pi,\pi]$.

items.q: The complex numbers $z_1=2-3i$, $z_2$ and $z_3$ are roots of $p(z)=z^3-8z^2+29z-52$. Find $z_2$ and $z_3$.
items.sol:
Real coefficients, so the conjugate is also a root: $z_2=2+3i$.
Sum of roots $=8$: $z_3=8-(2-3i)-(2+3i)=4$.
Check with the product: $(2-3i)(2+3i)\cdot4=13\cdot4=52$ ✓.

items.q: Find the square roots of $21-20i$.

Points $A(z_1)$ and $B(z_2)$ on an Argand diagram satisfy $OA=2\,OB$ and $\angle AOB=\frac{\pi}{6}$, with $B$ anticlockwise from $A$. Also $z_1=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, $0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}$.
(i) Express $z_2$ in exponential form in terms of $r$ and $\theta$. [2]
(ii) $C$ is the point such that $ABOC$ is a parallelogram and $\angle AOC=\phi$, $0<\phi<\frac{\pi}{2}$. $C$ is represented by $z_1w$. By finding $w$, calculate $\phi$ to two decimal places. [3] (The original has a diagram; open the paper to see it.)
items.sol:
(i) $|z_2|=\frac r2$ and $\arg z_2=\theta+\frac\pi6$, so $z_2=\frac r2 e^{i(\theta+\pi/6)}$.
(ii) Opposite sides are equal and parallel: $\overrightarrow{OC}=\overrightarrow{BA}$, so $z_1w=z_1-z_2=re^{i\theta}\left(1-\tfrac12e^{i\pi/6}\right)$.
So $w=1-\tfrac12e^{i\pi/6}=\left(1-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)-\tfrac14 i$, and $\arg w=-\tan^{-1}\frac{1/4}{1-\sqrt3/4}\approx-0.42$.
$C$ is clockwise from $A$ by $|\arg w|$, so $\phi\approx0.42$ radians.

items.q:
Consider the region defined by $|z-2+2i|\le4$ and $-\frac{\pi}{3}\le\operatorname{Arg}(z-1+3i)\le\frac{\pi}{4}$.
(i) Sketch the region. [3]
(ii) Let $w$ be any complex number in the region. Find the possible range of $\operatorname{Arg}(w)$, to two decimal places. [3]
items.sol:
(i) A disc with centre $2-2i$ and radius 4, cut by two rays from the excluded point $1-3i$ at angles $\frac\pi4$ and $-\frac\pi3$. The region is the slice of the disc between the rays.
(ii) The minimum is approached at the vertex $1-3i$ itself. That point is excluded, so the minimum is never reached: $\operatorname{Arg}(1-3i)\approx-1.25$.
The maximum is where the $\frac\pi4$ ray ($y=x-4$) meets the circle: $(x-2)^2+(x-2)^2=16\Rightarrow x=2+2\sqrt2$, $y=-2+2\sqrt2$, with $\operatorname{Arg}\approx0.17$.
So $-1.25<\operatorname{Arg}(w)\le0.17$.

items.q:
Let $C=1+\cos\theta+\cos2\theta+\dots+\cos(n-1)\theta$ and $S=\sin\theta+\sin2\theta+\dots+\sin(n-1)\theta$, with $z=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.
(i) Show that $C+iS=\dfrac{1-z^n}{1-z}$, $z\ne1$. [2]
(ii) Hence show that $\sin\theta+\sin2\theta+\dots+\sin(n-1)\theta=\dfrac{(\sin\theta-\sin n\theta)+\sin[(n-1)\theta]}{2(1-\cos\theta)}$. [2]
items.sol:
(i) By De Moivre, $C+iS=1+z+z^2+\dots+z^{n-1}$, a geometric series with ratio $z\ne1$, so it equals $\frac{1-z^n}{1-z}$.
(ii) Multiply top and bottom by $1-\bar z$. The denominator is $|1-z|^2=(1-\cos\theta)^2+\sin^2\theta=2(1-\cos\theta)$.
The numerator is $(1-z^n)(1-\bar z)=1-\bar z-z^n+z^{n-1}$, using $z\bar z=1$.
Its imaginary part is $\sin\theta-\sin n\theta+\sin(n-1)\theta$. Equate imaginary parts to get $S$.

items.q:
Let $\operatorname{Im}(z)\ne0$. Which is equivalent to $\dfrac{8\bar z z}{(\bar z-z)^2}$?
(A) $2+2\left(\frac{\operatorname{Re}z}{\operatorname{Im}z}\right)^2$   (B) $2+2\left(\frac{\operatorname{Im}z}{\operatorname{Re}z}\right)^2$   (C) $-2-2\left(\frac{\operatorname{Re}z}{\operatorname{Im}z}\right)^2$   (D) $-2-2\left(\frac{\operatorname{Im}z}{\operatorname{Re}z}\right)^2$
items.sol:
Let $z=x+iy$. Then $\bar zz=x^2+y^2$ and $(\bar z-z)^2=(-2iy)^2=-4y^2$.
So the expression is $\frac{8(x^2+y^2)}{-4y^2}=-2-2\left(\frac xy\right)^2$. (C)

items.q:
Let $z=5-12i$ and $w=3+4i$. Find:
(i) $v$ such that $3\bar v=z-2\bar w$ [2]
(ii) $\dfrac2w+z$ [1]
(iii) $u$ such that $u$ is a square root of $zw$, in the form $a+ib$ with $a>0$. [3]
Find $k\in\mathbb R$ so that there are only two points of intersection between $\left|\operatorname{Arg}(z-k-i)-\frac{\pi}{6}\right|\ge\frac{\pi}{6}$ and $|z-2-2i|=1$.
items.sol:
The inequality means $\operatorname{Arg}(z-(k+i))\ge\frac\pi3$ or $\le0$. So the region is everything except the wedge $0<\operatorname{Arg}(z-(k+i))<\frac\pi3$ with vertex $A=k+i$.
The circle (centre $2+2i$, radius 1) touches $\operatorname{Im}z=1$ at $B=2+i$. For only two intersections, the circle must sit inside the wedge, tangent to both rays.
By symmetry the centre is on the bisector, so $\angle BAC=\frac\pi6$ and $AB=\frac{1}{\tan(\pi/6)}=\sqrt3$.
So $k=2-\sqrt3$.

items.q:
(i) Using De Moivre's theorem, prove that $\cos6\theta=32\cos^6\theta-48\cos^4\theta+18\cos^2\theta-1$. [3]
(ii) Hence, by substituting $x=A\cos\theta$ for suitable $A$, or otherwise, find all roots of $P(x)=x^6-6x^4+9x^2-2$. [3]
items.sol:
(i) Take the real part of $(c+is)^6$: $\cos6\theta=c^6-15c^4s^2+15c^2s^4-s^6$. Substitute $s^2=1-c^2$ and simplify to $32c^6-48c^4+18c^2-1$.
(ii) With $x=2\cos\theta$: $P=64c^6-96c^4+36c^2-2=2\cos6\theta$.
So $P=0\iff\cos6\theta=0\iff\theta=\frac{\pi}{12},\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{5\pi}{12},\frac{7\pi}{12},\frac{3\pi}{4},\frac{11\pi}{12}$.
Roots: $x=\pm2\cos\frac{\pi}{12},\ \pm\sqrt2,\ \pm2\cos\frac{5\pi}{12}$, i.e. $\pm\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{2},\pm\sqrt2,\pm\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{2}$.

items.q:
A complex number $z$ satisfies $z^5+i=0$, $z\ne-i$.
(i) Show $z^4-iz^3-z^2+iz+1=0$. [1]
(ii) Prove $(z+i)\left(z^2+2iz\sin\frac{\pi}{10}-1\right)\left(z^2-2iz\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}-1\right)=0$. [3]
(iii) Hence prove $\sin\frac{\pi}{10}-\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}=-\frac12$. [2]
(iv) Hence find the exact values of $\sin\frac{\pi}{10}$ and $\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}$. [3]
items.sol:
(i) $z^5+i=(z+i)(z^4-iz^3-z^2+iz+1)$, and $z\ne-i$.
(ii) The roots of $z^5=-i$ are $e^{i\alpha}$ with $\alpha=-\frac\pi2,-\frac\pi{10},\frac{3\pi}{10},\frac{7\pi}{10},-\frac{9\pi}{10}$.
Pair $-\frac\pi{10}$ with $-\frac{9\pi}{10}$: their sum is $-2i\sin\frac\pi{10}$ and product $e^{-i\pi}=-1$.
Pair $\frac{3\pi}{10}$ with $\frac{7\pi}{10}$: their sum is $2i\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}$ and product $-1$. This gives the two quadratics.
(iii) Let $a=\sin\frac\pi{10}$, $b=\sin\frac{3\pi}{10}$. Compare $z^3$ coefficients: $2i(a-b)=-i\Rightarrow a-b=-\frac12$.
(iv) Compare $z^2$ coefficients: $-2+4ab=-1\Rightarrow ab=\frac14$. Solving gives $a=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}$ and $b=\frac{\sqrt5+1}{4}$.

items.q: Use the substitution $t=\tan\frac{\theta}{2}$ to find $\displaystyle\int\operatorname{cosec}\theta\,d\theta$.
items.sol:
$\sin\theta=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}$ and $d\theta=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}$.
So $\int\frac{1+t^2}{2t}\cdot\frac{2}{1+t^2}\,dt=\int\frac{dt}{t}=\ln|t|+C=\ln\left|\tan\frac\theta2\right|+C$.
(The official solutions in this paper are handwritten scans near the back.)

items.q: By using an appropriate $t$-formula substitution, solve $3\cos\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)-\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)=-3$ for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.
items.sol:
Let $t=\tan\frac{\theta}{4}$. Then $\cos\frac\theta2=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$ and $\sin\frac\theta2=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}$.
$3(1-t^2)-2t=-3(1+t^2)\Rightarrow-2t=-6\Rightarrow t=3$, so $\frac\theta4=\tan^{-1}3$ and $\theta\approx5.00$.
Test the excluded case: $t$ is undefined at $\frac\theta4=\frac\pi2$, i.e. $\theta=2\pi$. There, $3\cos\pi-\sin\pi=-3$ ✓.
So $\theta\approx5.00$ or $\theta=2\pi$.

items.q: Using the substitution $t=\tan\frac{x}{2}$, solve $2-3\sin x+2\cos x=0$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$. Round to two decimal places where necessary.
items.sol:
$2(1+t^2)-6t+2(1-t^2)=0\Rightarrow4-6t=0\Rightarrow t=\frac23$, so $x=2\tan^{-1}\frac23\approx1.18$.
Test $x=\pi$ (where $t$ is undefined): $2-0+2(-1)=0$ ✓.
So $x\approx1.18$ or $x=\pi\approx3.14$.

items.q: Use the substitution $t=\tan\frac{\theta}{2}$ to solve $2\sin\theta+\cos\theta=2$ for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$.
items.sol:
$4t+(1-t^2)=2(1+t^2)\Rightarrow3t^2-4t+1=0\Rightarrow t=1$ or $t=\frac13$.
So $\theta=\frac\pi2$ or $\theta=2\tan^{-1}\frac13\approx0.644$.
Check $\theta=\pi$: $0-1\ne2$, so it's not a solution.

items.q: By making the substitution $t=\tan\frac{\theta}{2}$, or otherwise, show that $\operatorname{cosec}\theta+\cot\theta=\cot\frac{\theta}{2}$.
items.sol: $\operatorname{cosec}\theta+\cot\theta=\frac{1+t^2}{2t}+\frac{1-t^2}{2t}=\frac{2}{2t}=\frac1t=\cot\frac\theta2$.

items.q: Solve $2\operatorname{cosec}\theta-4\cot\theta=3$ using the $t$-formula, for $0\le\theta\le2\pi$. Give answers to 3 significant figures.
items.sol:
$\frac{1+t^2}{t}-\frac{2(1-t^2)}{t}=3\Rightarrow3t^2-3t-1=0\Rightarrow t=\frac{3\pm\sqrt{21}}{6}$.
For $t\approx1.264$: $\theta\approx1.80$. For $t\approx-0.264$: $\frac\theta2$ is in the 2nd quadrant, so $\theta\approx5.77$.
$\theta=\pi$ is excluded because $\operatorname{cosec}\pi$ is undefined. Answers: $1.80,\ 5.77$.

items.source: North Sydney Boys 2025 Ext 1 Task, Q12(b)
items.q:
(i) Use $t$-formulae to show $\dfrac{1-\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}$. [1]
(ii) Hence find the exact value of $\tan15^\circ$. [1]
items.sol:
(i) $\dfrac{1-\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}}{\frac{2t}{1+t^2}}=\dfrac{2t^2}{2t}=t=\tan\frac\theta2$.
(ii) With $\theta=30^\circ$: $\tan15^\circ=\dfrac{1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}}{\frac12}=2-\sqrt3$.

items.q:
(i) Let $t=\tan\left(\frac x2\right)$. Prove that $\frac12\cot\left(\frac x2\right)-\cot x=\frac12\tan\left(\frac x2\right)$. [2]
(ii) Prove by induction for all $n\ge1$: $\frac12\tan\frac x2+\frac14\tan\frac x4+\dots+\frac1{2^n}\tan\frac x{2^n}=\frac1{2^n}\cot\frac x{2^n}-\cot x$. [3]
items.sol:
(i) $\frac1{2t}-\frac{1-t^2}{2t}=\frac{t^2}{2t}=\frac t2$.
(ii) $n=1$ is part (i). Assume the result for $n=k$ and add $\frac1{2^{k+1}}\tan\frac x{2^{k+1}}$.
Apply (i) with $x\to\frac x{2^k}$ and multiply by $\frac1{2^k}$: $\frac1{2^{k+1}}\tan\frac x{2^{k+1}}=\frac1{2^{k+1}}\cot\frac x{2^{k+1}}-\frac1{2^k}\cot\frac x{2^k}$.
The $\frac1{2^k}\cot\frac x{2^k}$ terms cancel, leaving $\frac1{2^{k+1}}\cot\frac x{2^{k+1}}-\cot x$ ✓.

items.q: By use of a product-to-sum identity, find $\displaystyle\int\cos2x\sin3x\,dx$.
items.sol:
$\sin A\cos B=\frac12[\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)]$ with $A=3x$, $B=2x$: $\cos2x\sin3x=\frac12(\sin5x+\sin x)$.
So the integral is $-\frac1{10}\cos5x-\frac12\cos x+C$.

items.q: Find $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin5x\cos3x\,dx$.
items.sol:
$\sin5x\cos3x=\frac12(\sin8x+\sin2x)$.
$\frac12\left[-\frac{\cos8x}{8}-\frac{\cos2x}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2}=\frac12\left[\left(-\frac18+\frac12\right)-\left(-\frac18-\frac12\right)\right]=\frac12$.

items.q: Find $\displaystyle\int3\cos(2x)\cos\left(5x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)dx$.
items.sol:
$\cos A\cos B=\frac12[\cos(A+B)+\cos(A-B)]$: the integrand is $\frac32\left[\cos\left(7x-\frac\pi3\right)+\cos\left(3x-\frac\pi3\right)\right]$.
So the integral is $\frac3{14}\sin\left(7x-\frac\pi3\right)+\frac12\sin\left(3x-\frac\pi3\right)+C$.

items.q: Use the product to sum identity to write $\cos\theta\sin(2\theta)$ as a sum in simplest form.
items.sol: $\sin2\theta\cos\theta=\frac12[\sin3\theta+\sin\theta]$.

items.source: North Sydney Girls 2026 Ext 1 Trial, MC Q7
items.q: How many distinct solutions does $\sin x+\sin3x=\sin2x$ have for $0\le x\le2\pi$? (A) 5 (B) 6 (C) 7 (D) 8
items.sol:
Sum-to-product: $\sin3x+\sin x=2\sin2x\cos x$, so $\sin2x(2\cos x-1)=0$.
$\sin2x=0$ gives $x=0,\frac\pi2,\pi,\frac{3\pi}2,2\pi$ (5 solutions). $\cos x=\frac12$ gives $\frac\pi3,\frac{5\pi}3$ (2 solutions). They're all distinct, so 7. (C)

items.q:
(i) Prove that $\cos5x-\cos x=-2\sin2x\sin3x$. [2]
(ii) Hence solve $\cos5x-\cos x=\sin3x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$, giving exact answers. [3]
items.sol:
(i) $\cos(A+B)-\cos(A-B)=-2\sin A\sin B$. With $A=3x$, $B=2x$ this gives the result.
(ii) $-2\sin2x\sin3x=\sin3x\Rightarrow\sin3x(1+2\sin2x)=0$.
$\sin3x=0$: $x=0,\frac\pi3,\frac{2\pi}3,\pi$. $\sin2x=-\frac12$: $2x=\frac{7\pi}6,\frac{11\pi}6$, so $x=\frac{7\pi}{12},\frac{11\pi}{12}$.

items.q:
Let $\underset{\sim}{u}=2\underset{\sim}{i}+5\underset{\sim}{j}$ and $\underset{\sim}{v}=-3\underset{\sim}{i}+\lambda^2\underset{\sim}{j}$, $\lambda\in\mathbb R$.
(i) Find $\lambda$ such that $u$ and $v$ are perpendicular. [2]
(ii) Explain why $u$ cannot be parallel to $v$. [2]
(iii) If $\lambda=1$, find $q$ such that $u=\operatorname{proj}_v(u)+q$. [3]
items.sol:
(i) $u\cdot v=-6+5\lambda^2=0\Rightarrow\lambda=\pm\sqrt{6/5}$.
(ii) Parallel would need $\frac{-3}{2}=\frac{\lambda^2}{5}$, i.e. $\lambda^2=-\frac{15}2<0$. That's impossible for real $\lambda$.
(iii) $v=-3i+j$ and $u\cdot v=-1$, $|v|^2=10$, so $\operatorname{proj}_v u=-\frac1{10}v=0.3i-0.1j$.
So $q=u-\operatorname{proj}_vu=1.7i+5.1j$ (check: $q\cdot v=-5.1+5.1=0$ ✓).

items.q:
$P,Q$ have position vectors $\underset{\sim}{p},\underset{\sim}{q}$; $\overrightarrow{QR}=\frac32\overrightarrow{OP}$; $M$ is the intersection of $PQ$ and $OR$ with $PM:MQ=\lambda:1$ and $OM:MR=\mu:1$.
(i) Show $\overrightarrow{OM}=\frac{\mu}{\mu+1}\left(\frac32p+q\right)$. [1]
(ii) Show $\overrightarrow{OM}=p+\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+1}(q-p)$. [1]
(iii) Prove $\lambda=\frac23$ and hence $\overrightarrow{OM}=\frac35p+\frac25q$. [3] (The original has a diagram.)
items.sol:
(i) $\overrightarrow{OR}=q+\frac32p$, and $M$ divides $OR$ in the ratio $\mu:1$.
(ii) $M$ divides $PQ$ in the ratio $\lambda:1$.
(iii) $p,q$ are non-parallel, so equate coefficients. For $q$: $\frac{\mu}{\mu+1}=\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+1}$. For $p$: $\frac32\cdot\frac{\mu}{\mu+1}=1-\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+1}=\frac1{\lambda+1}$.
So $\frac32\lambda=1$, giving $\lambda=\frac23$, and $\overrightarrow{OM}=p+\frac25(q-p)=\frac35p+\frac25q$.

items.source: North Sydney Boys 2025 Ext 1 Task, Q12(d)
items.q: Solve $5\cos\left(x+\tan^{-1}\frac43\right)=0.5$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$, correct to 2 decimal places.
items.sol:
$\cos(x+\alpha)=0.1$ with $\alpha=\tan^{-1}\frac43\approx0.9273$, and $x+\alpha\in[\alpha,2\pi+\alpha]$.
$x+\alpha=\cos^{-1}0.1\approx1.4706$ or $2\pi-1.4706\approx4.8126$.
So $x\approx0.54$ or $x\approx3.89$.
